prompt: After his family left West Philadelphia, where did Walter E. Williams spend much of his childhood?

choices.text: Chicago’s Cabrini-Green
North Philadelphia’s Richard Allen housing projects
Harlem’s Lenox Terrace
Atlanta’s Techwood Homes

explain: Williams was born in Philadelphia in 1936. His father was not part of raising him. The family later moved to the Richard Allen projects. He tells that story in his autobiography.
source: Up from the Projects: An Autobiography; biographical note on walterewilliams.com

prompt: Where did Williams earn his economics PhD, and what was the dissertation?

choices.text: The University of Chicago in 1968. The dissertation is Capitalism and Freedom
Harvard in 1975. The dissertation is The Affluent Society
UCLA in 1972. The dissertation is The Low-Income Market Place
George Mason in 1980. The dissertation is The State Against Blacks

explain: He took a BA in economics from California State College at Los Angeles in 1965, then an MA and a PhD from UCLA. George Mason is where he later taught. The State Against Blacks is a 1982 book, not the dissertation.
source: UCLA Economics memorial; about page on walterewilliams.com

prompt: Which post did Williams hold from 1980 until his death?

choices.text: Hoover Institution senior fellow who never taught undergraduates
Chair of the Council of Economic Advisers under Reagan
Tenured professor at Temple University for the whole period after 1980
John M. Olin Distinguished Professor of Economics at George Mason University, and department chair from 1995 to 2001

explain: He taught at Temple before 1980, then joined George Mason in 1980 and chaired economics there from 1995 to 2001. He kept teaching at George Mason through his last class in 2020.
source: About page on walterewilliams.com; UCLA Economics memorial

prompt: Which claim does The State Against Blacks argue most directly?

choices.text: Government rules such as minimum wages, occupational licensing, and entry limits have often blocked Black economic progress
Private markets are the main barrier to Black employment, so licensing should expand
Discrimination is impossible once a law mentions race
Only federal jobs programs can raise Black incomes

explain: The book treats the state as a barrier to Black economic progress. Chapters cover the minimum wage, taxicab medallions, and licensing in trades such as plumbing.
source: The State Against Blacks (1982). Commentary’s review of the book summarizes those chapters

prompt: In Williams’s minimum-wage argument, what happens when the law requires a wage above what a worker’s hourly output is worth to the employer?

choices.text: Employers hire more of those workers because the wage is now fair
Output rises on its own to match the legal wage
Hiring that worker becomes a loss, so the job often disappears
The wage floor creates a surplus of vacancies for the least skilled

explain: He asks the employer’s question. If you must pay a legal minimum to anyone you hire, you do not hire someone who produces less than that per hour. He treats the result as unemployment for the least skilled.
source: Column “Race and Economics” on walterewilliams.com; The State Against Blacks, the chapter reviewers call “Minimum Wage, Maximum Folly”

prompt: What does Williams argue about the Davis-Bacon Act of 1931?

choices.text: It abolished union wages so Black contractors could underbid anyone
It applied only to farms and never mentioned construction
He treats it as a minor rule with no labor-market effect
Its prevailing-wage rule on federal construction was debated in terms that targeted lower-paid Black labor, and he says Black workers then largely left those projects

explain: In his columns he points to the legislative debate, including members of Congress and the AFL president objecting to Southern contractors who used lower-paid Black workers. He argues the law then shut those workers out of federal construction.
source: Columns “Race and Economics” and “Minimum Wage and Discrimination” on walterewilliams.com

prompt: Which claim is closest to the thesis of South Africa’s War Against Capitalism?

choices.text: Free markets created apartheid and needed more central planning to undo it
Apartheid, including job-reservation laws, worked against market pressures that would have put Black workers into jobs reserved for whites
Job-reservation laws were unnecessary because no white employer would hire a Black worker
The book defends apartheid as a capitalist policy

explain: Williams argues apartheid was not a product of free markets. Job-reservation laws existed, in his account, because some employers would have hired Black workers at lower wages. He says racists could not trust markets to keep the color bar.
source: South Africa’s War Against Capitalism (Praeger, 1989); column “Discrimination and Segregation” on walterewilliams.com

prompt: A city caps rents far below the market to create “affordable” housing. Which reaction matches Williams?

choices.text: Expect a shortage, and a market that stays costly for people who cannot get a controlled unit. He makes the same point about 1970s gasoline price controls
Expect builders to add apartments because the cap makes tenants richer
Treat the shortage as proof the cap was set too high
Conclude that housing demand does not respond to price

explain: In “Compassion Versus Reality” he says rent controls aimed at affordable housing, and price controls aimed at price-gouging, produce a worse mess. He names San Francisco and New York as costly rent-controlled markets and recalls the 1970s gasoline lines.
source: Column “Compassion Versus Reality”; column “Gas Prices and Price Controls” (Capitalism Magazine, 2005)

prompt: After a demand spike, a legislature freezes the price of flour below the market. Which pattern does Williams’s price-control lesson predict?

choices.text: Farmers plant more because the freeze guarantees them a loss
Shortages prove the ceiling was above the market price
Millers and farmers have less reason to expand output, so flour runs short and black markets appear
A legal ceiling raises the quantity supplied

explain: In Economics for the Citizen he uses a flour ceiling as the example. If the controlled price does not pay for extra output, suppliers do not expand, and people trade at illegal prices.
source: Economics for the Citizen, Part V (FEE; also Capitalism Magazine)

prompt: A city requires an expensive taxi medallion before anyone can drive a cab. A poor person owns a used car and wants to start. What is Williams’s licensing argument?

choices.text: The high price means more poor people will enter, because the license is a status good
Occupational licensing raises employment for the least skilled
Only safety rules matter, so entry limits have no income pattern
The medallion blocks a bottom rung that used to be open. He contrasts an earlier New York, where a used car was enough, with later medallion prices that shut poor entrants out

explain: The State Against Blacks treats taxicab licensing in New York, Philadelphia, and Washington as an entry barrier. A 1982 review of the book reports his contrast. In the 1920s a poor person could start with a used car. By the time of the book, a New York license cost about $60,000.
source: The State Against Blacks, taxicab chapters; Commentary review (1982) reports the used-car versus $60,000 contrast

prompt: A council raises the wage floor above what many teenagers can produce in an hour, and says the law will help them. Which follow-up matches Williams?

choices.text: Ask only whether the council meant well
Ask which teenagers an employer will still hire once their output is worth less than the mandated wage
Assume employment of the least skilled rises one-for-one with the wage
Treat a later drop in teen jobs as proof the wage was set too low

explain: He separates intention from effect. A higher floor, in his account, makes it a loss to hire a worker who produces less than the legal wage per hour. He argues the harm lands hardest on low-skilled teenagers.
source: The State Against Blacks (“Minimum Wage, Maximum Folly”); column “Race and Economics”

prompt: Group A earns more than Group B. An advocate says the gap itself proves discrimination and nothing else. Which reply is closest to Williams?

choices.text: A gap proves that markets have already erased every legal barrier
Discrimination has never existed, so stop counting incomes
A gap has many possible causes. His 2011 book asks how much can be blamed on discrimination, and he also asks which laws price out the least skilled
Only genetics can explain a gap, so ignore law and skills

explain: Race and Economics: How Much Can Be Blamed on Discrimination? refuses the leap from unequal outcomes to one cause. The State Against Blacks adds a second question. Which rules cut the jobs and licenses the least skilled could have used?
source: Race and Economics: How Much Can Be Blamed on Discrimination? (2011); The State Against Blacks

prompt: A government bans Black workers from skilled mine jobs and says employers would never have hired them anyway. What question does Williams ask?

choices.text: The ban proves markets want racial job reservation
A lower wage offer is too minor to discuss, so the law changed nothing
Job reservation is what free entry looks like
If employers already refused, why was a law required? He argues some would have hired Black workers at a lower wage, so the color bar needed the state

explain: In “Discrimination and Segregation” he notes South African job-reservation laws for work such as running elevators and supervising machinery. He argues racists cannot trust free markets to keep those jobs white.
source: Column “Discrimination and Segregation”; South Africa’s War Against Capitalism

prompt: Supporters of a new licensing exam say it protects the public. The written section is unrelated to the work, and people who pass the practical test still fail it. What would Williams stress?

choices.text: A written test that people fail is proof the trade is safer
Effect can diverge from intention. An entry exam can screen out competent poor and minority applicants even when the stated goal is safety
Intention is the only result that matters
Licensing always increases the number of practitioners

explain: Reviewers of The State Against Blacks describe his Missouri beautician example. Applicants faced a written portion and a performance portion. The written portion, not the practical one, drove a racial gap in who passed. His point is the effect of the rule.
source: The State Against Blacks, occupational licensing; Reason, June 1983, summarizes the Missouri beautician exam
